clue.text: The Wind in the Willows, for example, may require explanatory statements

definitions.text: The Wind in the Willows, for example, may require explanatory statements

parts.words: The Wind in the Willows, for example, may require explanatory statements
parts.note: Kenneth Grahame's novel is a story told about life on a riverbank, while a holding at a bank is what monthly statements explain

explanation.surface: A literary critic suggests a children's classic needs some explanatory notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'account' as a narrative: The Wind in the Willows tells of Ratty and Mole by the riverbank, so it is a riverside account; the second half is the banking sense, where statements are sent out.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase works both as a story about a river's edge and as the money arrangement for which a bank posts regular statements.

clue.text: Close-ups of celebrities

definitions.meaning: in film jargon, tight close camera framings of a face

explanation.definitionFit: Film-makers call enlarged camera framings big shots, and very important people are informally called big shots too.

clue.text: Captain Nemo's craft with a marine creature

definitions.meaning: the submarine in Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
a sea-dwelling cephalopod with a spiral chambered shell

explanation.surface: Jules Verne's hero sails his submarine alongside a sea animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne named Nemo's submarine after the shelled cephalopod of that name, so one word covers vessel and animal.

clue.text: In the style of a second American mission

parts.note: à la is the French-derived phrase meaning in the manner of
a mo is a moment, a very short time

explanation.surface: Someone describes a fresh American undertaking modelled on an earlier one.
explanation.walkthrough: The Alamo was a Spanish mission in San Antonio, Texas, famous for the 1836 siege.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo began as a Spanish Franciscan mission station in Texas, later the site of a famous battle.

clue.text: Royal Court site arrived by chance

parts.note: came is the past tense of come, so it means arrived
lot means chance or fate, as in casting lots

explanation.surface: Someone stumbled upon the location of a royal court by luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal Court' suggests the London theatre, but here it is King Arthur's court.
explanation.definitionFit: In legend King Arthur held his court at this castle, home of the Round Table.

clue.text: Economic recovery at university, to fluctuate

parts.note: being up means in residence at a university, a British usage
to swing is to move back and forth or vary

explanation.surface: A campus economist watches a market bounce around as it recovers.
explanation.definitionFit: An upturn in business activity or prices is called an upward swing.

clue.text: Ditch insect biting

parts.note: a trench is a long narrow ditch
an ant is a common insect

explanation.surface: An insect in a ditch gives someone a nip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biting' looks like what the insect does, but it is the definition in its sense of sharp or cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: Biting criticism is incisive and sharp, the same quality as a cutting or keen remark.

clue.text: Visited some of the candidates

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is taken, so the run of letters sits inside them

explanation.surface: A canvasser called on a few of the people standing for election.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a place, informally, is to visit it as a tourist, so 'did' is past tense of that sense.

clue.text: Bunch of keys found in trash

parts.note: D, E, F, A, C and E are each a musical key, so a group of six of them spells out a word
D, E, F, A, C and E are each a musical key, so a group of six of them spells out a word
D, E, F, A, C and E are each a musical key, so a group of six of them spells out a word
D, E, F, A, C and E are each a musical key, so a group of six of them spells out a word
D, E, F, A, C and E are each a musical key, so a group of six of them spells out a word
D, E, F, A, C and E are each a musical key, so a group of six of them spells out a word

explanation.surface: A ring of keys turns up in the rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keys' suggests a door key and 'trash' rubbish, but the keys are musical ones named by letters, and 'trash' is a verb meaning to vandalise.
explanation.definitionFit: To trash something is to vandalise it, and to spoil its surface is to mar or vandalise it.

clue.text: Stone tomb of old-fashioned fellows

indicators.note: fashioned means shaped or made anew, so the letters of 'old' are reshaped

parts.note: men are fellows, chaps

explanation.surface: A stone burial chamber belongs to some traditional chaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old-fashioned' reads as one adjective, but it splits: 'old' is the fodder and 'fashioned' turns it into DOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehistoric megalithic structure of upright stones topped by a slab, thought to mark a burial chamber.

clue.text: A big cheese — a god, perhaps, around university?

indicators.note: around tells us the rearranged letters surround the university letter
perhaps hints that the letters of 'a god' may appear in another order

explanation.surface: An important campus figure is compared to a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns A GOD into GODA, and 'around' puts U inside it. 'A big cheese' looks like an important person but is literal: a large wheel of Dutch cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dutch variety of cheese, usually made in large rounded wheels.

clue.text: Domineering captain, almost saturated

parts.note: the master of a merchant ship is its captain

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: full means saturated, filled to capacity

explanation.surface: A bossy ship's skipper is nearly soaked through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims FULL to FUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone masterful takes control and imposes their will, like an overbearing commander.

clue.text: New Ohio poll, one con eludes, of the masses

indicators.note: concludes means the following piece comes at the very end
new suggests the letters are made over in fresh order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A fresh Ohio opinion survey finishes with a single verdict from ordinary people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges OHIO POLL into HOIPOLLO, and 'one concludes' adds I at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek phrase used in English for the common people, ordinary folk in general.

clue.text: Store of bread, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word is sounded rather than spelt

parts.note: bread is slang for money, i.e. cash

explanation.surface: Someone lists a supply of loaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bread' looks like a loaf but is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache is a hidden hoard, a stockpile kept for later use.

clue.text: One might go in a package

definitions.text: One might go in a package

parts.words: One might go in a package
parts.note: suggests a parcel's contents, but the package is a holiday deal bundling travel and hotel

explanation.definitionFit: A holidaymaker travelling on an all-inclusive holiday deal is a sightseer of this kind.

clue.text: At home, nursing has meaning

parts.note: in means at home, not out
tending means looking after, nursing

explanation.surface: Someone caring for a patient at home has a purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaning to do something is planning or having the purpose of doing it.

clue.text: Cheerful, good boy

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A well-behaved boy is in high spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Being pleased and happy is close to being cheerful.

clue.text: This shows how far 'e motored, roughly

indicators.note: roughly means approximately or not in the right form, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A Cockney driver's dashboard dial records the distance covered on his drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'e motored, a dropped-aitch 'he motored', supplies the letters EMOTORED to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's mileage instrument records the distance travelled.

clue.text: Wallop on top of gin is moonshine

indicators.note: in a down clue, on top of puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: to clap is to strike or slap, a wallop
a gin is a snare or trap for game

explanation.surface: A blow lands after too much gin, and the drink is illicit spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' and 'moonshine' both look like alcohol; gin is a trap, and moonshine means nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonshine can mean foolish talk, and pretentious empty talk is the same nonsense.

clue.text: Pupil's level twitch of the ear?

parts.note: an O level was the British school exam taken at about sixteen, so it is a pupil's level, giving O
a tic is a nervous twitch

explanation.surface: An eye's pupil and an odd twitch of the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupil' suggests the eye, but it is a schoolchild; O levels were British school exams before GCSEs.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical adjective for things relating to hearing organs, as aural is.

clue.text: Friendly drink

definitions.meaning: a sweet fruit-flavoured beverage, often diluted

explanation.definitionFit: The word means warm and amiable, and is also a sweet fruit syrup drink.

clue.text: Notice in French city, left behind the Bastille, possibly

indicators.note: behind puts the left letter after the rest
in places the notice inside the word for a city

parts.note: cité is French for city
an ad is a notice or advertisement

explanation.surface: A poster in a French town, abandoned near the Paris prison.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bastille was a Paris fortress used as a prison; 'possibly' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was a fortress, and a fortified stronghold guarding a town is this kind of building.

clue.text: Merry old king holding stage in Queen's, typically

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Old King Cole was a merry old soul in the nursery rhyme
a leg is a stage of a journey or race

explanation.surface: A jolly old monarch takes part in a play at the Queen's own residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen's' suggests the monarch, but Queen's is a college at Oxford and at Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen's at Oxford or Cambridge is a university institution of this type.

clue.text: Fifty cent cut is a big lump!

parts.note: fifty cents is half a dollar, so take half of the word dollar
to lop is to cut off

explanation.surface: A half-dollar reduction is a big chunk of savings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifty cent' gives half of DOLLAR, its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollop is a shapeless mass or large spoonful of something soft.

clue.text: Like Van Gogh's night? Take a second to linger

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
to tarry is to linger or delay

explanation.surface: An art lover pauses a moment in front of Van Gogh's nocturne.
explanation.walkthrough: Van Gogh painted The Starry Night (1889); the question mark marks the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's painting shows a sky full of stars swirling over a village.

clue.text: Decimal recurring much of the time

definitions.meaning: a decimal system is based on ten, so read as two words it is a reckoning in tens

explanation.surface: A maths student keeps meeting repeating decimals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recurring' suggests a recurring decimal, but it belongs to the second definition: something frequent.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two the word reads as a phrase meaning in tens; whole, it means frequently.

clue.text: I feel pram wobbling-that shows the lie of the land

definitions.text: that shows the lie of the land

indicators.note: wobbling means shaking unsteadily, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A parent feels a pram rocking on uneven ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lie of the land' is literal here: the terrain's hills and valleys.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart showing hills and valleys by shading or raised contours depicts the land's terrain.

clue.text: Quits, in spite of having succeeded?

parts.note: even is used to stress something surprising, as in 'even so', i.e. in spite of that
S is an abbreviation for succeeded, used in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone calls it a draw despite having won.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' is a link joining the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: When neither side owes the other anything, the score is level, quits.

clue.text: Vicar lied about what polished off the grub

indicators.note: about means around or in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clergyman fibbed about who finished off the food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'polished off the grub' reads as eating up food, but grub is an insect larva and polished off means killed.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemical killing insect larvae, the grubs, is a pesticide of this type.

clue.text: One hiring out property has no right to go inside

indicators.note: has no means the following letter is taken away

parts.note: a renter is one who lets or hires out property

explanation.surface: A landlord has no right to come into the flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has no' drops R from RENTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To go into a room is to come in or step inside.

clue.text: Settle party right away

indicators.note: away means removed, so those letters go out of the word

parts.note: taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: Someone sorts out a political party without delay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'away' drops RT from PARTY.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a bill is to hand over the money owed.

clue.text: Dispensing drugs openly as a baking ingredient

indicators.note: dispensing means handing out, suggesting the letters are spread out in a new order

explanation.surface: A pharmacist doles out medicine in full view, used as an ingredient in a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: GOLDEN SYRUP is a British pale treacle used in baking.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale treacle used in cakes and flapjacks is a sweet ingredient for bakers.
